c.tagline: The golden heart of Burgundy, serving Gothic spires, world-class wine, and its namesake mustard.

taxi.fareNote: Official taxis are metered; ranks at the train station and Place Darcy, or call ahead as street hailing is uncommon

emergency.note: 112 works EU-wide for any emergency and reliably connects to English-speaking dispatchers

avoid.reason: The Grésilles quarter has a rougher reputation after dark, and pickpockets work the station area; otherwise usual awareness.

hood_desc: Dijon's dense, largely pedestrianized old town, built around the Palace of the Dukes of Burgundy and threaded by the Owl's Trail (Parcours de la Chouette). Gothic and Renaissance mansions, the Notre-Dame church, and the covered market Les Halles are all within a short walk.

Once the quarter of wine merchants and boatmen along the Ouche canal, now Dijon's liveliest area for bars, small restaurants, and a lively Saturday market. It retains a rougher, more bohemian edge than the polished old town nearby.
A modern commercial district anchored by the Toison d'Or shopping center, one of the region's largest malls. Mostly of interest for chain shopping and a multiplex cinema rather than sightseeing.
A quiet, largely residential neighborhood northwest of the center, popular with families for its parks and easy tram access. Few tourist sights, but a good gauge of everyday Dijon life.

The university and science-campus district on the city's eastern edge, home to student housing, the botanical Jardin des Sciences, and Dijon's stadium. Quiet outside term time, livelier when students are in session.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout the city.

landmarks: Palais des Ducs de Bourgogne
The grand palace of Burgundy's dukes commands the city centre, its classical facades wrapping medieval halls, ducal kitchens and the fine arts museum.
Musée des Beaux-Arts de Dijon
Inside the ducal palace, one of France's oldest museums dazzles with the gilded, mourner-lined tombs of Philip the Bold and John the Fearless.
Église Notre-Dame and the Owl (La Chouette)
A 13th-century Gothic jewel bristling with gargoyles, whose small stone owl on the north side is rubbed with the left hand for luck.
Tour Philippe le Bon
Climb 316 steps up the dukes' 46-metre watchtower for the definitive panorama over Dijon's glazed-tile roofs toward the vineyard hills.
Les Halles de Dijon
A Gustave Eiffel-inspired 19th-century iron market hall where Burgundian producers pile cheeses, jambon persillé and mustard, gloriously lively on market mornings.
Cathédrale Saint-Bénigne
Dijon's Gothic cathedral, roofed in Burgundian polychrome tiles, conceals a haunting circular Romanesque crypt from the year 1001.
Place de la Libération
A graceful 17th-century semicircular royal square by Versailles architect Jules Hardouin-Mansart, now a fountain-splashed stage facing the ducal palace.
Rue des Forges and Maison Millière
Dijon's medieval showpiece street lines up half-timbered facades and Gothic mansions, including the 1483 Maison Millière crowned by a cat and owl.
Puits de Moïse (Well of Moses)
At the Chartreuse de Champmol on the city's edge, Claus Sluter's six life-sized prophets form a pinnacle of medieval European sculpture.
Cité Internationale de la Gastronomie et du Vin
A former hospital reborn as a temple to French food culture, with exhibitions, tastings, cooking schools and a vast Burgundy wine cellar.

train.note: Gare de Dijon-Ville is a ten-minute walk west of the Palais des Ducs. Paris Gare de Lyon is about 1h40m away by TGV, and there is a slow TER alternative taking around 3 hours for a fraction of the price. Three TGV Lyria trains a day continue from Dijon to Lausanne in about 2 hours, the city's only direct international service; Lyria tickets are sold through SNCF Connect and the booking window opens a few months ahead, with the cheapest fares going early. For Geneva, Basel or Zurich you change at Paris, Mulhouse or Lausanne. Dijon also has direct TGVs to Charles de Gaulle airport, which is often quicker than routing through central Paris.

bus.note: Long-distance coaches use the bus station beside Dijon-Ville railway station, so connections between train and coach are easy. Regional Burgundy services run under the Mobigo brand and cover Beaune, Dole and the Cote d'Or wine villages, with tickets sold at a flat regional fare on board or online. International coaches take far longer than the train - Geneva is about 4 hours by bus - so they are worth it mainly on price. Book FlixBus and BlaBlaCar Bus online, as neither sells tickets at a staffed desk here.

ferry.note: Dijon is landlocked in eastern France and has no passenger ferry services. The Burgundy Canal and the Saone carry hotel barges and self-drive hire boats from the Port du Canal south of the centre, but these are holiday cruises rather than scheduled transport. The nearest sea ferries are on the Mediterranean, five hours or more away.

half.name: Beaune
half.blurb: Burgundy's wine capital, home to the colorfully tiled Hôtel-Dieu hospice and cellars along the Côte d'Or wine route.

half.name: Autun
half.blurb: Roman-founded town with a well-preserved Gallo-Roman gate, amphitheater ruins, and a Romanesque cathedral known for its carved capitals.

half.name: Besançon
half.blurb: Fortified city on a bend of the Doubs River, crowned by Vauban's UNESCO-listed Citadelle overlooking the old town.
